keyTakeaways: PowerPoint or Keynote can remain a sensible choice for a short, fixed surtitle sequence with one display and a rehearsed operator.
A purpose-built live workflow becomes more valuable when the production needs direct cue selection, blackout control, fast recovery, or multiple audience delivery paths.
Translated surtitles and same-language captions answer different audience needs; neither projection nor phone delivery is automatically accessible to everyone.
SurtitleLive can assist with script preparation and structured cue operation, but the production team remains responsible for text, timing, translation approval, rehearsal, and fallback planning.

faq.question: When is PowerPoint suitable for theatre surtitles?
faq.answer: A slide deck can work well for a short, stable cue list on one display when the operator has enough preparation and rehearsal time. The production should still test skips, repeats, blackouts, and its agreed fallback.

faq.question: When should a production consider purpose-built surtitling software?
faq.answer: Consider it when the show needs direct cue selection, recovery without exposing the search to the audience, coordinated language tracks, or both projected and personal-device outputs.

faq.question: Does delivering captions to phones make a performance accessible?
faq.answer: Not by itself. Phone delivery can offer language choice and individual viewing, but it also depends on devices, battery, network access, and digital confidence. Productions should explain those requirements and plan a reasonable alternative where needed.

faq.question: What role does AI play in SurtitleLive script preparation?
faq.answer: AI can help identify dialogue and speakers and create an editable draft. It does not make the production's editorial decisions: people still review extraction, line breaks, names, translations, and performance timing.

glossary.definition: A prepared unit of text that an operator selects for display at the appropriate moment in a performance.
A deliberate control that hides the audience text while the operator searches, recovers, or follows an agreed show action.
Prepared text that helps an audience understand dialogue performed in another language.
Text in the performance language that may also identify speakers and convey meaningful sound information.
The practical route through which an audience reads the text, such as a shared projection, a personal device, or a planned combination.
